people.label: David Fravor
people.sub: CDR, USN (Ret.); Commanding Officer, VFA-41 Black Aces; 14 Nov 2004 Nimitz intercept
people.narrative: Fravor is the aviator whose single intercept broke the observational record open. In November 2004 he was Commanding Officer of Strike Fighter Squadron Forty-One, the Black Aces, attached to Carrier Air Wing Eleven aboard USS Nimitz. In his sworn written statement to the House Oversight Subcommittee on National Security, the Border and Foreign Affairs on 26 July 2023 he described being vectored off a training intercept to investigate a contact the cruiser USS Princeton had been tracking, and finding 'a small white Tic Tac shaped object with the longitudinal axis pointing N/S and moving very abruptly over the white water,' with 'no Rotors, No Rotor wash, or any visible flight control surfaces.' He testified the Princeton had been watching objects descend from above 80,000 feet to 20,000 feet 'for the previous 2 weeks.' The single most load-bearing line in his statement is a negative one: 'the incident was never investigated, none of my crew were ever questioned, tapes were never taken.' That sentence is not a denial of the coverup - it is evidence of the specific shape of it. The Navy's own range fouler report on the incident, released via FOIA on 13 January 2023, records that 'Reporting terminated at 3rd Fleet, there was no process to share the reporting.' The event stayed dormant until Jay Stratton contacted Fravor in 2009 to investigate it for a DoD program, and until the New York Times published the FLIR1 video in December 2017. Fravor told 60 Minutes on 16 May 2021 the object 'was aware we were there' and that 'it just disappears. Like, gone.'
affiliations: Carrier Air Wing Eleven / USS Nimitz (2004)
people.tierRationale: Tier A: the primary aviator witness of the founding modern incident, on the record under oath with a written statement in the congressional record, corroborated by a FOIA-released Navy range fouler report.

people.label: Alex Dietrich
people.sub: LCDR, USN (Ret.); VFA-41 wingman on the 14 Nov 2004 Nimitz intercept
people.narrative: Dietrich was the second F/A-18F aircrew on the 14 November 2004 intercept, flying as Fravor's wingman and observing the object for roughly five minutes. She is named alongside Fravor in the Navy's own range fouler report on the incident, released through the Navy FOIA reading room on 13 January 2023 - which matters because it puts her at the event in a government record rather than only in a media account. She stayed silent publicly for sixteen years, then gave her first public account on CBS 60 Minutes on 16 May 2021, opening with 'I never wanted to be on national TV, no offense.' That reluctance is itself the datum: the stigma structure the ODNI's own June 2021 preliminary assessment described - 'disparagement associated with observing UAP, reporting it, or attempting to discuss it with colleagues' - operated on her for a decade and a half. Mike Gold, testifying before House Oversight on 13 November 2024, cited her by name, saying she 'was mocked by her colleagues' and that her incident 'went years without any investigation.' Dietrich has since argued in print for cooperative, data-first investigation rather than advocacy, publishing an opinion piece in The Debrief on 17 February 2023.
affiliations: Naval Postgraduate School / Pentagon staff tours
people.tierRationale: Tier A: named in a FOIA-released Navy range fouler report as aircrew on the founding incident, and a first-person on-the-record witness whose silence-then-speech is documentary evidence of the reporting stigma.

people.label: Kevin Day
people.sub: Senior Chief Operations Specialist / Air Warfare Coordinator, USS Princeton (CG-59), Nov 2004
people.narrative: Day was the Senior Chief Operations Specialist running the air picture in USS Princeton's combat information center during the two weeks of contacts that culminated in the 14 November 2004 intercept. His role is the load-bearing one for the radar side of the case: the Princeton's SPY-1B, freshly upgraded, was the sensor that established the objects were descending from above 80,000 feet, that they were numerous, and that they were not tracks the Aegis library recognised. Fravor's own sworn statement to House Oversight corroborates the substance of Day's picture - that Princeton 'had been observing these objects on their Aegis combat system for the previous 2 weeks' descending 'from above 80,000ft ... rapidly down to 20,000ft.' Day has said publicly in documentary and broadcast interviews that within a day or two of the intercept, personnel who did not identify themselves arrived aboard Princeton and removed recording media, and that he was told to stop discussing it. That confiscation account is the pivot of the whole coverup strand for this incident and it has not yet been anchored to a primary record - no FOIA release, no visit log, no message traffic identifying the personnel or the authority under which they acted has surfaced. It is recorded here as a tier-2 attributed account with the primary-record gap stated plainly, because a fabricated citation would destroy exactly the claim that most needs to survive audit.
affiliations: US Navy (retired Senior Chief Operations Specialist)

people.label: Gary Voorhis
people.sub: Petty Officer, CEC/Aegis computer and radar technician, USS Princeton (CG-59), Nov 2004
people.narrative: Voorhis was a Cooperative Engagement Capability and Aegis systems technician aboard USS Princeton in November 2004, which put him at the exact node where the incident's machine record lived - the tapes and drives that captured what the SPY-1B and the CEC network saw. His public account, given repeatedly in documentary and broadcast interviews from 2018 onward, is that in the days after the intercept he was directed to hand over or wipe recording media, including data-tape cartridges, and that personnel he did not recognise were aboard doing the collecting. If accurate, it is the cleanest single instance of the program's evidence-handling behaviour in the entire modern aviator record: not a denial, not a classification decision anyone signed in public, but a physical removal of the primary sensor product within days. It has not been corroborated by any released document. The Navy has never produced Princeton radar data for 14 November 2004, and the FOIA-released range fouler report for the incident says only that reporting 'terminated at 3rd Fleet.' Voorhis is carried at tier C precisely because the claim is important enough that it must not be over-graded.
people.tierRationale: Tier C: on-the-record named witness in the right technical billet, but every specific of his confiscation claim is currently uncorroborated by primary documents.

people.label: Ryan Graves
people.sub: Lt, USN (Ret.), VFA-11 Red Rippers; Executive Director, Americans for Safe Aerospace
people.narrative: Graves converted the 2014-2015 USS Theodore Roosevelt workup encounters from an anecdote into an institutional safety problem, which is why he is the aviator the disclosure movement could not be talked out of. In his written statement to House Oversight on 26 July 2023 he testified: 'In 2014, I was near Virginia Beach as part of VFA-11, a Navy Fighter/Attack Squadron made up of F/A-18F Super Hornets,' and that his squadron 'began witnessing advanced UAP demonstrating complex maneuvers on a regular basis' after the fleet upgraded to the APG-79 AESA radar. The pivotal event he described occurred in Warning Area W-72, 'an exclusive block of airspace ten miles east of Virginia Beach,' where 'one of the pilots saw a dark gray cube inside of a clear sphere - motionless against the wind, fixed directly at the entry point,' and two jets 'only 100 feet apart, were forced to take evasive action.' The institutional failure is the part that indicts: 'Our squadron submitted a safety report, but there was no official acknowledgement of the incident and no further mechanism to report the sightings.' Two of the three videos the Department of Defense formally released on 27 April 2020 - GIMBAL and GO FAST, both filmed in January 2015 - came out of this operating area. Graves founded Americans for Safe Aerospace to build the reporting channel the Navy did not provide, telling Congress in July 2023 that it had 'nearly 5,000 members' and was 'actively working with more than 30 UAP witnesses.'

people.label: Timothy Gallaudet
people.sub: Rear Admiral, USN (Ret.); former Oceanographer of the Navy; former acting NOAA Administrator
people.narrative: Gallaudet is the flag officer who put the safety-of-flight coverup into the congressional record in the first person. Testifying before the joint House Oversight subcommittees on 13 November 2024, he described a January 2015 email from the operations officer of US Fleet Forces Command to all subordinate commanders with the subject line 'URGENT SAFETY OF FLIGHT ISSUE.' The email carried the GO FAST video and, in Gallaudet's account, asked: 'If any of you know what these are, tell me ASAP. We are having multiple near-midair collisions, and if we do not resolve it soon, we will have to shut down the exercise.' The next day, he testified, the email disappeared from his account and from other recipients' accounts without explanation. His conclusion in sworn written testimony is the sharpest available statement of the mechanism: the information 'must have been classified within a special access program managed by an intelligence agency.' This is the single most useful witness account on the board for the question of authority, because it describes not a leak or a rumour but an administrative action taken against an official Navy safety communication - a recall of a fleet-wide flight-safety warning. Gallaudet was Commander, Naval Meteorology and Oceanography Command in 2015, later Oceanographer of the Navy, then Assistant Secretary of Commerce and acting NOAA Administrator.

people.label: Alexandro Wiggins
people.sub: Senior Chief Petty Officer (Operations Specialist), USN; USS Jackson (LCS-6) witness, 15 Feb 2023
people.narrative: Wiggins is the first active-duty Navy senior enlisted man to testify to Congress about a UAP encounter he personally supervised, and his case is the strongest post-Nimitz maritime datum on the board. In written testimony to the House Oversight Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets on 9 September 2025 he described an event on '15 February 2023 at approximately 1915 PST in the W-291 Warning Area off the Southern California coast.' A self-luminous tic-tac-shaped object emerged from the ocean and joined three others - four in total - with 'no visible control surfaces and no exhaust plume - features inconsistent with conventional aircraft.' Crucially, this one was recorded: USS Jackson's combat information center captured it on a Star SAFIRE multi-spectral electro-optical/infrared system, and the footage carries 'timestamps, lat/long, and platform readouts consistent with USS Jackson's location.' The chain here is the thing to watch. The video did not reach the public through the Navy or through AARO; it reached the public through journalists Jeremy Corbell and George Knapp, and Wiggins then went to Congress under his own name while still serving. Nineteen years after the Nimitz, the same operating areas, the same object description, the same institutional silence - and the record moves only when a witness carries it out himself.

people.label: Jeffrey Nuccetelli
people.sub: USAF veteran, security forces / military police, Vandenberg AFB 2003-2005
people.narrative: Nuccetelli brought the base-security side of the observational record into the congressional record. In written testimony to the House Oversight Task Force on 9 September 2025 he described serving as military police at Vandenberg Air Force Base, home of the National Missile Defense project, and receiving reports on 14 October 2003 from Boeing contractors of 'a massive, glowing red square silently hovering over two missile defense sites.' The same night, security guards reported a bright fast-moving object and witnesses described 'a massive rectangular craft, larger than a football field.' A week later a patrol reported an object over the ocean that descended and 'vanished instantly into the night sky'; in 2005 a patrol reported 'a massive triangular craft, larger than a C-130, hovering low over the main base.' Two things make this testimony operationally significant rather than anecdotal. First, he states that 'Official Air Force records documenting it are now held by AARO and the FBI' - which is a specific, checkable custody claim that FOIA can be aimed at. Second, he states one witness 'was threatened and told to keep quiet about the incident,' which is the same suppression pattern the Navy witnesses describe, applied to a strategic missile installation.

people.narrative: Borland testified before the House Oversight Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets on 9 September 2025 as an Air Force veteran UAP witness. people.label: Gregory M. Guillot
people.sub: General, USAF; Commander, NORAD and US Northern Command (Feb 2024- )
people.narrative: Guillot is the four-star who had to say out loud that the United States cannot identify what is flying over its own nuclear-capable bases. He took command of NORAD and US Northern Command in February 2024 and immediately made counter-unmanned-systems the centrepiece of his 90-day assessment, with the December 2023 Langley Air Force Base incursions as the driving case. Speaking to The War Zone on 30 October 2024 he conceded the limits of what he could say - 'The only thing I can tell you about the Langley drones is roughly the number and roughly the altitude' - and, on the question everyone wanted answered, 'I have not seen [and] I do not know of any organized or unorganized foreign nexus.' NORAD's own figure at that point was more than 600 drone reports over US military installations since 2022. entities.desc: The Aegis cruiser that generated the machine record of the November 2004 encounter and, on the accounts of two of its crew, then lost it. entities.desc: A sustained series of encounters during USS Theodore Roosevelt workups off the US East Coast, reported by VFA-11 and other Carrier Air Wing One aircrew from 2014 into 2015. The squadron filed a safety report and received no acknowledgement. That is the shape of the concealment on the aviator strand: not denial of the encounters, but suppression of the safety machinery that would have forced them into the open.

entities.label: July 2019 Drone Swarms, USS Kidd / USS Russell and CSG ships off California

entities.desc: Over multiple nights in July 2019, unidentified aircraft repeatedly operated over and around US Navy warships in the Southern California operating areas, and the Navy's own deck logs record it. entities.desc: Beginning the evening of 6 December 2023, unidentified unmanned aircraft operated over Joint Base Langley-Eustis, home of front-line F-22 Raptors, and continued through the month. Seventeen nights of unidentified aircraft over a stealth fighter base, and no attribution has ever been made public.

entities.label: New Jersey and East Coast Drone Wave (Nov-Dec 2024)
entities.sub: Mass sighting wave; four-agency joint denial
entities.desc: From mid-November into December 2024 a wave of nocturnal drone sightings over New Jersey and neighbouring states produced more than 5,000 reports to the FBI and a political crisis. On 17 December 2024 the Department of Defense, Department of Homeland Security, FBI and FAA issued a joint statement: 'We have not identified anything anomalous, and do not assess the activity to date to present a national security or public safety risk over the civilian airspace in New Jersey or other states.' Officials said they had run down about 100 specific leads and found 'commercial drones, hobbyist drones, and law enforcement drones, as well as manned fixed-wing aircraft, helicopters, and stars mistakenly reported as drones.' First, the same assessment conceded 'limited' sightings over military facilities in restricted airspace, contradicting earlier White House statements that there had been none. Second, it landed while Wright-Patterson Air Force Base had closed its airspace for nearly four hours on 14-15 December over unauthorized drone activity. A four-agency statement that resolves 100 of 5,000 reports and generalises the result to all of them is not an investigation finding; it is a communications posture, and it is recorded here as one.

entities.label: February 2023 Alaska, Yukon and Lake Huron Shootdowns
entities.sub: Three unidentified objects destroyed by US fighters in four days
entities.desc: Between 10 and 12 February 2023, US fighters shot down three unidentified objects over Alaska, the Yukon and Lake Huron, in the days after the Chinese surveillance balloon was destroyed off South Carolina. A Secret memorandum dated 14 February 2023 from Janice Charette, Clerk of the Privy Council, to Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and National Security Advisor Jody Thomas records that 'The full exploitation of UAP #20, which was engaged by the U.S. on February 10, 2023, has not yet been completed,' describing an object roughly the size of a small car at 40,000 feet, 'cylindrical and silver-ish gray' with no apparent propulsion system, which broke apart on sea ice near Prudhoe Bay. The Yukon object, tracked as UAP #23, 'remains unverified' as to 'function, method of propulsion, or affiliation to any nation-state.' The Lake Huron object was destroyed on 12 February 2023 by an AIM-9X fired from one of two F-16CMs of the Minnesota Air National Guard's 148th Fighter Wing at roughly 20,000 feet; a pilot reported 'In the targeting pod, I can't tell if it's metallic or what, but I can see like lines coming down below it.' None of the three were recovered intact. Infrared footage of the Lake Huron engagement was not released until 22 May 2026, through the PURSUE initiative, and the source entry noted an unusual absence of 'substantiated chain-of-custody.' Sean Kirkpatrick's retrospective characterisation - 'We scrambled jets and shot down a bunch of things. Do you know what we shot down? Balloons' - is recorded here as a denial artefact, since the Canadian government's own contemporaneous Secret memo says the objects' function and propulsion were unknown.

entities.label: USS Ronald Reagan Encounter and Logbook Tampering (2003-2004)

entities.desc: Between December 2003 and May 2004, while USS Ronald Reagan (CVN-76) operated in the Atlantic, multiple watchstanders observed a round, orange, self-luminous object hovering roughly 100 to 200 feet above the flight deck, pacing the ship at about 22 knots and performing half-circle manoeuvres before departing rapidly. entities.desc: The Department's statutory annual UAP report covering 2 June 2024 to 30 May 2025, released on 20 July 2026 - roughly nine months late, and only about three months before the FY2026 report was due. It records 319 new reports (284 during the period and 35 from prior years), total holdings of 1,870 cases as of 30 May 2025, 370 cases resolved during the period (114 new and 256 from previous periods), 191 cases moved to an 'active archive' pending corroborating data, and 9 reports 'meriting further analysis' by intelligence and science and technology partners. On the aviator question the report makes two claims worth pinning: 'AARO did not receive reports indicating flight safety concerns during this reporting period,' and 'Two UAP reports described electronic or avionic interference as attributable to UAP in proximity to an operational aircraft.' Those two sentences are in tension, and the report resolves it by definition rather than by analysis. It also states 'To date, no evidence suggests that a USG or private entity has ever captured or exploited UAP-derived materials.' The report notes cases logged near sensitive military installations and critical infrastructure with 'performance characteristics exceed the known state-of-the-art' while adding 'No technical data accompanied these reports' - which is a statement about the reporting pipeline, not about the objects. The report is issued under the Department of War, reflecting the departmental renaming.

entities.label: Charette Privy Council Memorandum (Secret, 14 Feb 2023)
entities.sub: Canadian government memo on the February 2023 shootdowns
entities.desc: A Secret memorandum dated 14 February 2023 from Janice Charette, Clerk of the Privy Council, to Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and National Security Advisor Jody Thomas, obtained and reported by The War Zone on 7 September 2023. It is the most authoritative contemporaneous government document on the February 2023 shootdowns, and it directly contradicts the tidy retrospective account that they were all balloons. Charette wrote that 'The full exploitation of UAP #20, which was engaged by the U.S. on February 10, 2023, has not yet been completed' - an object described as roughly the size of a small car, at 40,000 feet, 'cylindrical and silver-ish gray' with no apparent propulsion system, which broke apart on frozen sea ice near Prudhoe Bay. Of the Yukon object, tracked as UAP #23, she recorded that it 'remains unverified' as to 'function, method of propulsion, or affiliation to any nation-state,' adding 'It is unknown whether it poses an armed threat or has intelligence collection capabilities.' The memo also conceded recovery was unlikely given terrain and snow. The numbering itself is significant: two allied governments were tracking a sequential UAP series in which these were entries 20 and 23.

entities.label: Fleet Forces Command 'URGENT SAFETY OF FLIGHT ISSUE' Email (Jan 2015, recalled)
entities.sub: Recalled Navy fleet-wide safety message carrying the GO FAST video
entities.desc: A January 2015 email from the operations officer of US Fleet Forces Command to all subordinate commanders, subject line 'URGENT SAFETY OF FLIGHT ISSUE,' attaching the GO FAST video and asking: 'If any of you know what these are, tell me ASAP. We are having multiple near-midair collisions, and if we do not resolve it soon, we will have to shut down the exercise.' Then-Rear Admiral Tim Gallaudet, at the time Commander of Naval Meteorology and Oceanography Command, testified in writing to the House Oversight joint subcommittees on 13 November 2024 that the email disappeared from his account and from other recipients' accounts 'without explanation' the very next day, and that he concluded the information 'must have been classified within a special access program managed by an intelligence agency.' This document - or rather its deletion - is the single sharpest artefact of the concealment mechanism in the aviator record. It is not a classification decision anyone defended, not a refusal to comment, not a denial: it is the retroactive removal of an official Navy flight-safety warning from every recipient's inbox. No agency has acknowledged ordering it, and the message identifier, sender and recall authority remain unidentified.

entities.label: House Oversight Task Force Hearing: Restoring Public Trust Through UAP Transparency and Whistleblower Protection
entities.sub: 9 September 2025, HVC-210
entities.desc: Held on 9 September 2025 in HVC-210 by the House Oversight Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets, chaired by Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, this was the first congressional UAP hearing built around serving and former operators rather than programme officials. The witnesses were Jeffrey Nuccetelli (USAF veteran, Vandenberg AFB), Senior Chief Alexandro Wiggins (active-duty Navy, USS Jackson), Dylan Borland (USAF veteran), journalist George Knapp, and, as minority witness, Joe Spielberger of the Project On Government Oversight. Wiggins's appearance is the structural break: an active-duty senior enlisted man testifying under his own name about a sensor-recorded encounter his service had not publicly assessed. Knapp told the panel the public has been told since the late 1940s 'there's nothing to worry about here' while documents show military personnel acknowledging 'these things are real. They're not fictitious.' Wiggins framed the issue as safety first: 'When crews observe objects that maneuver in ways that do not match known profiles ... that is first and foremost a safety issue.' Members Burchett, Burlison, Perry and Mace pressed on whistleblower protection, cross-agency documentation, and whether the government had run psychological operations on the subject.

entities.label: Southern California Operating Areas (W-291 and Baja approaches)
entities.sub: US Navy warning areas, Pacific
entities.desc: The block of Pacific warning areas and range complexes off Southern California and the Baja approaches in which the two most significant American maritime UAP encounters occurred nineteen years apart. Carrier Strike Group 11 was working up here in November 2004 when USS Princeton tracked objects descending from above 80,000 feet and VFA-41 intercepted the Tic Tac roughly 30 miles off Baja California. The July 2019 drone swarms against USS Kidd, USS Rafael Peralta, USS Russell and USS John Finn occurred in the same operating environment. On 15 February 2023, USS Jackson recorded four transmedium tic-tac objects in Warning Area W-291. The geographic persistence is a datum in itself: three distinct classes of event - a single high-performance object, a coordinated multi-platform swarm, and a transmedium group - concentrated in the same instrumented, heavily surveilled naval training space over two decades, with the Navy's own range fouler reporting confirming the first and its own deck logs the second.

entities.label: Warning Area W-72, off Virginia Beach
entities.sub: Restricted Atlantic training airspace
entities.desc: An exclusive block of restricted airspace ten miles east of Virginia Beach used for air combat training, and the site of the near-midair that anchors Ryan Graves's congressional testimony. Graves described it as 'an exclusive block of airspace ten miles east of Virginia Beach' where 'one of the pilots saw a dark gray cube inside of a clear sphere - motionless against the wind, fixed directly at the entry point,' with two F/A-18Fs 100 feet apart forced into evasive action. The location matters because it is not open ocean: it is controlled, deconflicted airspace whose entire purpose is that nothing uninvited is in it. An object holding station against the wind at the entry point of a live training area is either a catastrophic airspace-control failure or an intrusion, and in either case it generated a squadron safety report that the Navy, per Graves, never acknowledged. The Atlantic warning areas are also the environment that produced GIMBAL and GO FAST in January 2015 and, per Gallaudet, the recalled Fleet Forces Command safety message about 'multiple near-midair collisions.'

entities.label: Joint Base Langley-Eustis, Virginia
entities.sub: F-22 Raptor base; site of the December 2023 incursions
entities.desc: Home to front-line F-22 Raptors and, from the evening of 6 December 2023, the site of the most consequential unattributed airspace intrusion on US soil in the modern record. The Air Force confirmed 'multiple incursions throughout the month of December' by unmanned aircraft that 'ranged in size/configuration' and fluctuated in number. The response - F-16 combat air patrols with tanker support, NASA WB-57F high-altitude surveillance orbits, FBI coordination through NORTHCOM - is not what a base does about hobbyists. Gen. Mark Kelly described at least one drone as roughly 20 feet long at more than 100 mph and 3,000 to 4,000 feet. F-22s were relocated, and by October 2024 the Air Force was evaluating protective netting for the aircraft. Gen. Gregory Guillot made Langley the centrepiece of his 90-day counter-UAS assessment on taking NORAD/NORTHCOM command in February 2024 and stated he knew of no foreign nexus. Langley is also where the aviator strand and the incursion strand converge: the same restricted airspace regime that failed to identify the 2004 and 2015 objects failed again, at home, over a stealth fighter base, for seventeen nights.

entities.label: Barksdale Air Force Base, Louisiana
entities.sub: B-52 bomber base; March 2026 incursion waves
entities.desc: A nuclear-capable B-52 bomber base that in March 2026 became the focal point of the most serious domestic incursion episode yet recorded. On 9 March 2026 the base raised force protection to FPCON Charlie and issued a shelter-in-place order after reports of an unmanned aerial system over the installation; Capt. Hunter Rininger, chief of public affairs, confirmed the report and the FAA's involvement. Reporting later that month described multiple waves of 12 to 15 drones over sensitive areas including the flight line, with non-commercial signal characteristics, resistance to jamming, and flight patterns suggesting the operators were probing security responses - all of it occurring after the launch of Operation Epic Fury, the US bombing campaign against Iran flown in part by Barksdale's B-52s. Only one Anduril counter-drone fly-away kit was fielded at the time and the bombers remained largely exposed on the flightline. Barksdale is the point where the fourteen-month-old federal position that drone sightings were hobbyists and misidentified stars became untenable.

claims.source: Capt. Hunter Rininger, Barksdale AFB Public Affairs, 9 March 2026

entities.label: NORAD and US Northern Command
entities.sub: Homeland air defence combatant command
entities.desc: The command responsible for detecting and defeating air threats to North America, and the institution whose public statements since 2023 constitute the government's most damaging admissions on the observational record. NORAD counted more than 600 drone reports above US military installations since 2022. Its commander since February 2024, Gen. Gregory Guillot, made counter-UAS the centrepiece of a 90-day assessment driven by the Langley incursions, established the Falcon Peak counter-drone demonstration series, and stated on the record that he knew of no 'organized or unorganized foreign nexus' to Langley. In February 2023 NORAD-controlled fighters destroyed three unidentified objects over Alaska, the Yukon and Lake Huron in four days, none of which were recovered intact and two of which an allied government's own Secret memorandum described as unverified as to function and propulsion. By March 2026 Guillot confirmed detections over installations had increased year on year with roughly a quarter defeated. A homeland air defence command that cannot attribute persistent intrusions over its own bomber and fighter bases is the strongest available argument that the observational record is a live national-security problem rather than a historical curiosity.

entities.label: USS Jackson (LCS-6)
entities.sub: Independence-class littoral combat ship
entities.desc: The littoral combat ship whose combat information center recorded four transmedium tic-tac-shaped objects in Warning Area W-291 off Southern California at approximately 1915 PST on 15 February 2023, using a Star SAFIRE multi-spectral electro-optical/infrared system. Senior Chief Operations Specialist Alexandro Wiggins testified to the House Oversight Task Force on 9 September 2025 that the footage carries 'timestamps, lat/long, and platform readouts consistent with USS Jackson's location' - metadata of exactly the kind the NASA Independent Study Team said the government's UAP holdings lack. The ship is significant to the board because of the disclosure path, not just the sighting: the recording reached the public through journalists, and the crew member carried it to Congress himself while still on active duty. No AARO case assessment of the Jackson footage has been published, and it is not identifiable in any released annual report.

nimitz-2004.desc: The 14 November 2004 encounter between Carrier Strike Group 11 and an unidentified object roughly 30 miles off Baja California is the founding event of the modern observational record, and this board treats it as the clearest available cross-section of how the concealment works in practice. Four things are documented beyond argument. First, the object existed and was described in an official Navy record: the range fouler report released via FOIA on 13 January 2023 calls it 'solid white, smooth, with no edges ... uniformly colored with no nacelles, pylons, or wings ... approximately 46 feet in length.' Second, it was tracked for two weeks by a US Navy Aegis cruiser descending from above 80,000 feet, per Fravor's sworn statement. Third, its infrared signature was captured by a US Navy targeting pod and, sixteen years later, the Department of Defense authenticated the footage while declining to explain it. Fourth, the reporting went nowhere: 'Reporting terminated at 3rd Fleet, there was no process to share the reporting.' Around that documented core sit two contested claims that pull in opposite directions. Fravor testified under his own name that 'the incident was never investigated, none of my crew were ever questioned, tapes were never taken.' Princeton crewmen Kevin Day and Gary Voorhis say recording media were removed by personnel who did not identify themselves within about 48 hours. Both can be true if collection was aimed at the ship's sensor archive rather than at the squadron - which would be the more sophisticated behaviour, not the less. What is certain is the outcome: two decades on, no Princeton radar data, no CEC recording, and no investigative file for the incident exists in any public release, while the object's own infrared portrait hangs in the Pentagon's press archive labelled 'unidentified.'

gallaudet-2015-email.desc: The recalled January 2015 US Fleet Forces Command message is the highest-value single artefact on the aviator strand, and it deserves separate treatment because of what it rules out. A refusal to comment is consistent with indifference. A classification decision is consistent with ordinary secrecy. But the retroactive deletion of an already-distributed fleet-wide flight-safety warning from the inboxes of every subordinate commander is not consistent with either. It requires that someone with authority over Navy messaging systems decided, within 24 hours, that a safety-of-flight warning about repeated near-midair collisions was more dangerous distributed than the near-midairs themselves. Gallaudet, a serving flag officer at the time and later acting NOAA Administrator, drew the only available inference in sworn testimony: the information 'must have been classified within a special access program managed by an intelligence agency.' The message is also the connective tissue between the two halves of the aviator record. It carried GO FAST - one of the three videos DoD later released as authentic and unidentified - and it described exactly the problem Ryan Graves's squadron was filing unacknowledged safety reports about in the same airspace in the same period. Nine years later, AARO reanalysed GO FAST on parallax grounds and concluded it showed nothing anomalous. That analysis, whatever its merits, has no bearing on why the warning was withdrawn. No agency has ever acknowledged withdrawing it, and the sender, message identifier and recall authority remain unidentified.

langley-2023-incursions.desc: The December 2023 Langley incursions are where the historical UAP record and the contemporary homeland-defence problem stop being separable. For at least seventeen nights beginning 6 December 2023, unidentified aircraft operated over a front-line F-22 base in Virginia. The response was not what an installation mounts against hobbyists: F-16 combat air patrols with tanker support, NASA's WB-57F high-altitude research aircraft flying surveillance orbits, FBI coordination routed through NORTHCOM. At least one object was described by Gen. Mark Kelly as roughly 20 feet long, moving at more than 100 mph at 3,000 to 4,000 feet. F-22s were moved; by October 2024 the Air Force was evaluating protective netting for the aircraft on the ground. And the commander of NORAD and US Northern Command, having made the incident the centrepiece of his 90-day assessment, said on the record that he knew of no organized or unorganized foreign nexus. The pattern then repeated and escalated: New Jersey in December 2024, met with a four-agency statement that resolved about 100 of more than 5,000 reports and generalised the result; UK bases in November 2024; a joint interagency task force in August 2025; an Inspector General finding in January 2026 that ten evaluated installations lacked coherent counter-drone authority; and in March 2026 waves of 12 to 15 jam-resistant drones over a nuclear-capable B-52 base during an active bombing campaign. Whatever these objects are, the record they generate is identical in shape to the record the 2004 and 2015 encounters generated: detected, tracked, unattributed, and officially minimised.

gaps: No primary record has been located for the alleged confiscation of USS Princeton recording media after 14 November 2004. Targets: Princeton quarterdeck and deck logs for 14-18 Nov 2004, any unscheduled embarkation record, CSG-11 message traffic, and the Aegis/CEC data retention schedule for that period. This is the single highest-value open item on the domain.

The identity of the US Fleet Forces Command operations officer who sent the January 2015 'URGENT SAFETY OF FLIGHT ISSUE' email, the message's date-time group or identifier, and the authority under which it was recalled from all recipients' accounts. A FOIA to Fleet Forces Command for message recall records in January 2015 has not been reported.

The VFA-11 squadron safety report filed after the Warning Area W-72 near-midair has never been released. Its Naval Safety Command hazard report control number is unknown, and no FOIA response confirming or denying its existence has been reported.

No AARO case assessment has been published for FLIR1 or GIMBAL, despite published assessments for GO FAST, Aguadilla (2013) and Mt Etna (2018). Whether assessments exist in classified form is unknown.

The USS Jackson (LCS-6) Star SAFIRE recording of 15 February 2023 has not been officially released and cannot be identified in any AARO annual report. Whether it was ever submitted to AARO, and under what case number, is unknown.

Jeffrey Nuccetelli testified that Vandenberg AFB records from 2003-2005 are 'now held by AARO and the FBI.' Neither agency has confirmed this. FOIA targets: 30th Space Wing security forces blotters for 14 Oct 2003, AFOSI files, and FBI records referencing Vandenberg overflights.
The chain of custody of the original FLIR1 tape between November 2004 and its unauthorized appearance in 2007 is entirely undocumented in public releases.

Chad Underwood's role in capturing FLIR1 is consistently reported but was not anchored to a verified primary or archival source in this research pass; his own published interviews need a stable citation.
The full unredacted DODIG-2026-045 report, the identities of the ten installations it evaluated, and JIATF-401's establishing directive, funding line and reporting chain are all unavailable.
The classified annexes of Gen. Guillot's 90-day counter-UAS assessment, and NORAD's per-installation incursion counts for 2025 and 2026, have not been released.

No official explanation exists for why NASA declined to name Mark McInerney as Director of UAP Research at the 14 September 2023 briefing, and no public output from that role has been identified in the three years since.

The USS Ronald Reagan deck logs for the 2003-2004 deployment should be checked against the witness accounts of pages being removed; if pages are missing or renumbered, that is a documentable destruction of federal records.

PURSUE releases 01 through 05 (8 May to 7 August 2026) have not been systematically indexed for aviator cases; SCU has documented metadata stripping but a case-by-case audit against the Navy range fouler set and AARO's holdings has not been done.
Jason Turner's rate, division and billet aboard USS Princeton in November 2004 are not established from any primary record, and his account has not been separately documented.
The 2019 USS Kidd/Russell investigation reportedly reached the Chief of Naval Operations. The resulting staff package, any NCIS or FBI case file, and the final disposition have never been released.
